gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 has a single DC input shared by car and solar. BLUETTI's Charger 1 alternator charger also plugs into that input through MC4. So on this station, roof solar and alternator charging work one at a time, not together, unless the shopper uses BLUETTI's Charger 2. Charger 2 takes up to 600 W of solar into the charger itself and merges it with alternator power into one feed.
standout_why: I read four cited pages: powersized.com/best/rv, solarpowerauditor.com/camping/best-power-station-rv-van, ecosolarkits.com/blogs/guides/best-rv-solar-kits and solargenadvisor.com. Solargenadvisor failed with an SSL error. Powersized gives the Elite 200 V2's 96 W car input and its 12–60 V, 20 A solar window. It also names Charger 1 at 560 W, but never says that Charger 1 uses the same single DC input as the panels. Solarpowerauditor says the car-socket circuit is limited to about 120 W and that a DC-DC charger is needed, but names no BLUETTI charger and says nothing about port sharing. Ecosolarkits mentions only Anker's 800 W alternator charger. None of the three mentions Charger 2 or charging from solar and alternator at once on one input. Our own page says 'Car socket only' for the Elite 200 V2, which is wrong: BLUETTI sells an Elite 200 V2 + Charger 1 bundle.
decides: This keeps the Elite 200 V2 as the pick but changes the kit we recommend. Charging while driving is not limited to the 96 W car socket. Charger 1 adds up to 560 W from the alternator ($219, or $1,099 bundled with the station), but it takes the station's only DC input, so the panel is disconnected while it is in use. A van with roof panels that also charges while driving should get Charger 2 ($429, or $1,299 bundled with the station, no panel included). Charger 2 takes up to 600 W of solar plus alternator power and sends both into the one input. The Elite 200 V2's own input limit of 1,000 W at 12–60 V, 20 A still applies. Our 'Charging while driving' cell for the Elite 200 V2 should change from 'Car socket only' to these options. The AC180 row already lists a Charger 1 bundle.

findings.label: DC inputs on the station
findings.value: 1 DC input, used for either a car or solar panels
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Review (Page 2 of 5) – A Closer Look, Hardware · APH Networks
findings.note: APH Networks wrote: 'Connections in the front include a DC input to charge the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 using your car or solar panels.' The review describes only one DC input. The AC input is a separate C14 inlet on the side.

findings.label: DC input limits
findings.value: Solar up to 1,000 W at 12–60 V, 20 A max; car input 96 W from 12 V or 192 W from 24 V; AC plus DC combined up to 2,400 W
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Review (Page 1 of 5) · APH Networks
findings.note: These are APH Networks' spec-table lines. StorageReview's review lists the same solar and car figures (storagereview.com, read 2026-11-14).

findings.label: How it connects, its power and its price
findings.value: Up to 560 W. The box includes a DC input cable and an MC4 output cable, so it feeds the station's solar/DC input. $219 (list $249), in stock
findings.note: Product text: 'delivers up to 560W of power— 6X faster than a traditional car charger... fully charge a 1kWh power station in just 2.5 hours.' The page says it 'Works with all BLUETTI power stations.' It does not name the station port it plugs into; the MC4 output is what puts it on the solar input. The price and stock status come from the store's product data via storecheck.
